newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU welcomes US move to drop grain dispute panel.
newsitem.headline: EU welcomes US move to drop grain dispute panel.

text.p: The European Commission on Tuesday welcomed a decision by the United States to drop a demand for a World Trade Organisation dispute panel on European Union grain tariffs.
"We were somewhat surprised when the U.S. asked for a panel as all the issues are being worked on. It doesn't make sense to ask for a panel at this time," Commission farm spokesman Gerard Kiely said.
Senior EU and U.S. agricultural officials are due to meet later on Tuesday to discuss trade disputes ranging from a veterinary standards agreement through rice and malting barley imports.

Washington is concerned that an estimated $2.0 billion trade in veterinary and phytosanitary products could be disrupted when the EU harmonises import rules in the 15 member states on January 1, 1997.

Some $250 million of petfood, $120 million of dairy products $115 million of meat, $150 million of live animals and $100 million of tallow and $300 million of fish products would be affected, U.S. officials said.

EU Commission officials have said that negotiations with the U.S. over mutual recognition of veterinary and plant health standards will not be concluded before the end-year deadline but have stressed trade will not be halted.
U.S. officials have warned against slipping into chaos.
"There are profound implications," said one official, stressing that many EU manufacturers were highly dependent on imports from the U.S.

On rice, Washington is exasperated at EU delay in implementing an agreement to import an extra 38,000 tonnes of milled rice and 8,000 tonnes of brown rice duty-free. The concession was introduced as compensation for trade losses after Austria, Sweden and Finland joined the EU in 1995.

The U.S. is also unhappy with the EU's reference price based system for calculating tariffs on normal rice imports and its failure to introduce a cumulative recovery system to claw back excess duties.
On malting barley, the EU has still to introduce a 30,000 tonnes a year duty-free quota.
